attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter post, not a quotation of someone else.

semantics.note: The firm, unhedged statement "aren't coming" is a forecast with no deadline. The scare quotes are kept as a sign of scepticism without narrowing the claim. This matches what he wrote.

contract.note: He named no measure, so the plain reading applies: useful delegated multistep tasks with limited supervision, in repeated real use. That is an ordinary reading of 'agents' in early 2025. It does not demand general or transformative agents, which would stretch the claim against him. The result depends on this reading.

evidence.note: METR, an independent evaluator, reported in May 2026 that its own engineers regularly let agents work alone for hours on multistep tasks. It also records failures and poor judgement. This is direct operational evidence from users other than the vendors.

December 2025 survey and case studies finding agents in production across many domains, but mostly constrained, under heavy human evaluation, and with reliability problems. It shows the limits of deployment and does not decide the case alone.

reviews.rationale: The early-resolution rule is met. METR's dated May 2026 report shows sustained, repeated use of agents carrying out useful multistep work with limited supervision. That use is by METR's own staff, not the vendors. Under the fair plain reading, the forecast that agents aren't coming is contradicted. The reliability limits in e1 and e2 qualify this but do not reverse it.

attribution.note: The claim rests on Zitron's own comment. Altman's quoted words only frame it.

semantics.note: An observation about the state of things up to the post date. It keeps both parts, 'yet to materialize' and 'or even come close', and his characterisation of Altman.

contract.note: Reading AGI as broad human-level competence is ordinary and fair. But 'come close' has no threshold, and the speaker gave none, so the result turns on how distance to AGI is judged. 'Always' is probably rhetorical.

evidence.note: The 2025 International AI Safety Report describes uneven capabilities and many limitations, and treats AGI as something in the future. This fits 'not yet materialized' but gives no measure of how close systems were.
ARC Prize (December 2024) calls o3 a major leap in generalisation, which weighs against 'not even close'. It is one benchmark and does not establish distance to AGI.

reviews.rationale: The evidence fits the narrow point that AGI had not arrived by January 2025. The contract's support condition also requires showing that OpenAI had not come close. The packet offers no agreed measure of that, and ARC's 'breakthrough' finding cuts the other way. The 'always' part about Altman is unverified. Neither the support nor the contradiction condition is met.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his post.

semantics.note: The firm part is the observation that GPT-4o cost around $100M to train. The o1 comparison is hedged ('would likely') and cannot be scored. The 'likely' modality should apply only to the o1 part.

contract.note: It is fair to require evidence specific to GPT-4o and to treat the o1 part as tentative. A GPT-4 figure is correctly ruled out as proof either way.

evidence.note: The linked 2023 WIRED piece is about GPT-4, not GPT-4o, and Altman says GPT-4 cost more than $100M. It concerns a different model, so it is context only.
Epoch AI (May 2025) says o1's training compute is unknown. It does not set o1's dollar cost or how it compares with GPT-4o.

reviews.rationale: No item in the packet gives a training cost for GPT-4o. The cited $100M figure concerns GPT-4, a different model, so it can neither support nor contradict the claim. The o1 comparison is hedged and cannot be scored in any case. The firm GPT-4o figure cannot be settled from this evidence.

attribution.note: Zitron's own statement of figures in his post.

semantics.note: The normalised claim keeps the 27% share, the roughly $1B ARR basis, and the roughly $2.7B from subscriptions.

contract.note: Holding him to the ARR basis he wrote himself is fair. Using calendar 2024 is a reasonable reading because he named no snapshot date. The result depends on whether projected annual revenue can stand in for ARR.

evidence.note: Fortune (September 2024) reports projections, not actuals: $3.7B of revenue in 2024, with $2.7B from ChatGPT and $1B from other businesses. That gives the 27% split, but on a projected full-year basis rather than ARR.

A September 2024 analysis repeats the projected split, roughly $1B (27%) API and $2.7B subscriptions. It gives a run rate of about $3.6B in August 2024 and estimates about $5B by year-end. These are estimates, not observed figures.
CNBC (June 2025) gives about $5.5B of total ARR for 2024, which is far from the implied $3.7B. It has no breakdown by component, and its wording about the snapshot is imprecise.

reviews.rationale: The figures match OpenAI's projected 2024 full-year revenue split. They do not match a verified ARR snapshot, which is the basis he stated. CNBC's $5.5B total ARR suggests a mismatch but gives no matching component breakdown. No consistent 2024 snapshot in the packet confirms or refutes all three figures on the stated basis.
